newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bank profits to slow,focus moves to mergers.
newsitem.headline: German bank profits to slow,focus moves to mergers.

text.p: German banks, fresh from posting healthy profit gains in the first nine months, will have a strong final quarter but the party could be over in 1997 when earnings growth may slow sharply, analysts said on Thursday.

They said that will increase pressure on banks to slash costs in their domestic retail businesses, likely to become their main focus in coming years after an expensive race into investment banking since 1994.

With banks desperate to make their cost-laden branch networks more efficient in a chronically overcrowded banking market, speculation about mergers is here to stay despite bankers' efforts to quash it, the analysts said.
"The central theme in the coming two years will be consolidation and linked to that, cost control," said Olaf Conrad, banking analyst at Morgan Stanley in London.
The speculation sent bank shares up sharply in heavy trading this week.

Germany's top five banks have reported operating profit rises of between 9.9 percent and 37 percent in the first nine months, buoyed by a bull run on bond and stock markets this year which has boosted trading and commission income.
Most banks expect a last fling in the final months of 1996.

They say trading income will pick up from a relatively weak third quarter while commissions will profit from the flotation of Deutsche Telekom, Europe's largest ever listing which has sparked a buying frenzy among traditionally equity-shy Germans.
But markets are expected to soften next year when Germany's economic upturn gains pace and the prospect of an interest rate increase, which looks remote at present, appears on the horizon.
"We won't see the huge earnings growth rates we had in 1996, that's impossible," said Konrad Becker, banking analyst at Merck, Finck in Frankfurt.
Analysts said net commission income was unlikely to rise much while trading profits would drop slightly. Stronger loan demand may boost interest income, however, they said.
Conrad said he had revised down his earnings estimates for 1997, particularly for the two largest German banks Deutsche Bank AG and Dresdner Bank AG.
He expects Deutsche earnings per share of 4.30 marks in 1996 and 1997. Dresdner's earnings per share will total 3.10 marks in 1996 and slip to 3.00 marks in 1997, Conrad said.
Meanwhile analysts are split on which banks to favour.
Some see Deutsche as a clear buy because of its determination to restructure its management and strengthen its London-based investment banking business under Morgan Grenfell.

Others are more impressed with the cost-cutting efforts of Commerzbank AG, the third-largest bank, which posted the strongest operating earnings rise of 36.9 percent and has cut its cost-income ratio to 64 percent, well below Deutsche and Dresdner.

"Commerzbank has good prospects and quite a respectable cost-income ratio," said Oliver Finger, banking analyst at DG Bank who rates Commerzbank as a "buy" and has "hold" recommendations for Deutsche and Dresdner.
But Sabine Bohn, an analyst at Schroeder Muenchmeyer Hengst in Frankfurt, rates Deutsche as buy.
"We think Deutsche has the best strategy in terms of investment banking and cost-cutting, although it won't shine through in earnings until 1998 or 1999," Bohn said.

Shares in the two Munich banks, Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG, have benefited most from merger speculation which gripped Germany after Deutsche said in July it had bought a 5.21 percent stake in Vereinsbank.

While Bohn has Vereinsbank as a buy, Conrad at Morgan Stanley sees both banks "hopelessly overvalued" from a fundamental point of view. He still rates the shares as neutral because they should remain propped by merger fever.
